props.title: The Wild World of Batwoman
props.initialSlug: Campy superhero romp with dancing crime-fighters

sections.content: The Wild World of Batwoman (1966) stands as one of cinema's most fascinating train wrecks, riding the coattails of the popular Batman TV series (1966) while narrowly avoiding copyright lawsuits. Director Jerry Warren, notorious for ultra-low-budget exploitation films like Teenage Zombies (1959), cobbled together this incoherent mess featuring Batwoman and her "Avenging Angels" fighting crime in go-go boots. The film gained renewed infamy when featured on Mystery Science Theater 3000 (1991) where its bizarre dance sequences, nonsensical plot about stolen atomic hearing aids, and baffling villain named Rat Fink became legendary fodder for mockery.

sections.content: The mid-1960s saw an explosion of unauthorized superhero knockoffs trying to capitalize on the Batman TV series phenomenon. Rat Pfink a Boo Boo (1966) started as a serious crime drama before randomly transforming halfway through into a superhero parody. The Wild World of Batwoman took this trend to its illogical extreme, with endless padding via stock footage and interpretive dance numbers. The film's legal troubles with DC Comics forced a re-release under the title "She Was a Hippie Vampire," though it contained neither hippies nor vampires.

Jerry Warren's filmmaking technique became a masterclass in how not to make movies. Like fellow Z-movie auteur Ed Wood with Glen or Glenda (1953), Warren padded his runtime with stock footage, interpretive dance sequences, and lengthy scenes of characters walking between locations. The sound mixing regularly drowns out dialogue with inappropriate jazz music, while the plot thread about atomic hearing aids seems to have been borrowed from a different script entirely. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Bad Cinema

movies.title: Catwoman
movies.slug: Halle Berry stars in this notorious DC Comics adaptation that swept the Razzie Awards

sections.content: While The Wild World of Batwoman is objectively terrible, it holds an important place in cult cinema history alongside films like Troll 2 (1990) and The Room (2003). These "so bad they're good" movies reveal the raw passion of filmmaking stripped of competence or resources. Warren's film particularly illuminates the 1960s exploitation market, where quick cash-grabs based on popular properties could find distribution despite their quality.
